content.thinking:
I'm planning out the module structure now, starting with constants and palette setup, then textures, helper functions for ear and tuft shapes, and finally the main build function, generating texture code for the tuft material.

Still writing SVG textures...

I'm working through the moss tuft blades, the flower petals and stem, and the glowing cyan rune design, deciding how colors and tints apply across colored versus grayscale elements.

For the hanging moss vines, since the card leans at 180 degrees (root edge up top), I realize I can just reuse the same moss tuft texture logic since both draw thick strand bases tapering to narrow tips.

For vines, I'll make a separate texture: a long strand shape wide at the base with tiny leaf bumps pointing upward.

Counting up the textures needed: eye, grey tuft, moss, vine, flower, rune makes six, plus maybe a cloth pattern for the scarf ribbon and a glowing leaf-in-circle emblem decal, bringing it to seven or eight.

Now I'm defining the rust paint color with a mottled texture...

Setting up more paint colors - dark shadows, cream highlights, deeper and paler rust tones, plus teal and gold accents for variety. Then I'm building the coat material using a fur-edge effect with toothy texture along the body.

Now starting the actual build function, naming it "redPanda" and considering paint resolution - thinking through whether 2048px is too large given the painted surface area, estimating texel density to decide if 1024 would suffice instead.

Setting up the root joint and spine chain using a catmull-rom curve through hip-to-chest points, naming the sub-joints hips/spine1/spine2/chest and assigning them a spine role within the body group.

I'm now building the neck chain similarly, spanning from chest up to a head tip joint, but I'm second-guessing how to assign a distinct "head" role since the tip joint is just the last link of the neck chain rather than its own independent joint — trying to figure out whether the naming convention alone covers the head role requirement.

Still defining spine geometry...

Setting up the leg geometry function, computing root and target joint positions for front legs relative to shoulder placement, and passing a bend direction vector into the limb builder to shape the knee bend.

I'm settling on unique joint names for front (shoulderL, elbowL, handL) and hind legs (hipL, kneeL, ankleL, footL), then sweeping each chain with tapered radius arrays for a smooth leg shape, using legPaint color and grouping them under "legs". For the paw, I'm placing a sphere at the tip joint's position with a small offset downward and forward.

Now I'm adding four toe spheres arranged in an arc at the paw's tip with slight flattening, plus small spike claws angled outward from each toe, and considering a slight outward splay rotation for a more natural paw stance before assigning a darker paw color.

Keeping toes dark rather than cream, skipping pad detail, and now sketching sparse fur tuft cards scattered along the spine and body surfaces, tinted with the coat color, to add texture around 70 instances along the back.

Moving to the tail, I'm building a curved chain from a root near the hips out through several joints, checking that the tail origin sits inside the body cleanly rather than floating outside it, then starting to define taper radii along its length.

Now I'm figuring out the tail's coloring, alternating rust and paler reddish-orange bands based on position along the tail with a dark tip, trying to get that subtle ringed look real red pandas have rather than strong contrasting stripes.

For the fur tufts on the tail, I'm scattering tuft cards along the surface with leaning and bending so they align with the tail's curve, aiming to have each card's direction follow the tail path's tangent at that point so the fur naturally flows along the bend.

For tinting, I realize the surface coordinates won't work for cards since there's no meaningful position there, so instead I'll color each card based on its closest point along the tail path, using the same ring-color function so the tufts blend seamlessly with the tail's surface pattern. Cards will shade using their own facing direction as the normal, then I'll move on to building the head.

I'm setting up the head's local coordinate helper and placing the skull as a scaled sphere geometry attached to the head bone, then deriving the skin surface from it before starting on the eyes using an anime-style iris color.

For the eyes, I'm raycasting against the skin surface on both sides to find placement points, then applying mirrored decals with appropriate size, direction, and lift so they sit correctly on the face. Now I'm moving to the snout, positioning it forward and down from the head center with its own scale and a cream-colored paint.

I'm adding the nose as a small dark sphere at the snout tip with a tiny highlight, then working out the mouth and lower jaw using scaled spheres in cream and darker tones for the interior.

Checking the vertical positions, I move the jaw down slightly so it protrudes properly below the snout without overlapping the skull, keeping the mouth interior tucked just above it.

Now I'm drafting the mouth seam line as a draped path along the snout's lower silhouette, defining a few swept points on each side and preparing to render it as a thin dark ink stroke.

For the ears, I'm computing the ear base position relative to the head joint, accounting for the skull's curvature to find the correct up/forward offset at a given side position, slightly behind center.

Still writing ear geometry...

Finishing the cheek ruff outline shape, I'm checking that it protrudes outward from the skull's half-width properly at that head height, and considering scaling it down slightly since 0.16 out from center seems a bit too large for the fluff effect.

Tracing through the notch points to confirm the outline stays non-self-intersecting, then mirroring the x-offset for the opposite side so it tilts backward symmetrically.

Now I'm figuring out the forehead tuft geometry, placing the three blade bases along the skull's front-top edge and sweeping bezier curves from base to tip with tapered radii.

I'm then designing the ahoge to curve forward-up like a Genshin-style hair spike, fanning three blades left, center, and right with the center one longer. For whiskers, I'm computing start and end points on each side of the snout and sweeping thin rods outward and slightly downward with a four-sided cross-section.

Now for the neck and scarf, I'm building a collar as a closed loop around the neck, sweeping a tube of teal cloth along it with the radius and tangent plane derived from the neck chain's position and weights.

I'm checking the geometry at this point along the neck — the tangent is tilted about 38° since the neck curves from chest to chin, so the collar loop plane needs to follow that tilt, and the cross-section radius there is roughly 0.098, close to the neck tube's own radius.

Good, this loop sits right at the base of the neck and the shoulders aren't being clipped, and the scarf stays tucked behind the head sphere so it's visible from the side without clipping. I'm adding gold trim loops near the top and bottom of the scarf band with thin tube radii, and planning the front knot as a small sphere where the tails hang down below the chin.

I need to figure out orientation on the tilted collar loop to find the front-center point — I'll find the closest point on the loop to a target forward-down position and use that to place the knot, then hang a small gold ring and medallion disc just below it, angled forward-down. For the ribbon tails trailing from the nape, I'm working out which angle on the loop corresponds to the back of the neck.

Still writing ribbon geometry...

Now I'm designing the medallion: a lathed gold outline profile mounted at an angle, with a glowing teal icosahedron gem at the front, skipping a rim ring for simplicity. I'm deciding to skip separate hanging cords and attach the medallion directly beneath the collar instead.

For the boulder, I'm using a lathe geometry with a custom rock-shaped point profile, flat-shaded for faceted normals, scaled wider in one axis to give it an irregular stone look.

Checking whether the paws would sit properly on the top plateau of the boulder - the ellipse math shows they're mostly inside but close to the edge, so I'm adjusting the lathe points to widen the flat top slightly.

Now I'm positioning two extra bump rocks using scaled icosahedron geometry, carefully nudging their y-centers up so they don't sink below the ground plane by more than a negligible amount.

Then I'm setting up the moss painting logic so clumps appear only on surfaces with sufficiently upward-facing normals, and scattering moss cards across the boulder and bumps while avoiding areas too close to the paw positions, using small leaning texture cards for the moss appearance.

For hanging vines, I'm building a rim loop around the boulder near the top, sampling points along that path to generate frames, randomly selecting a subset, and placing drooping vine cards at each one with a flowing downward orientation.

Settling on 0.035 lift for the vine loop. For flowers I'm scattering about 9 near the top rim away from the paws, varying size and avoiding overlap with the plateau edge. For mushrooms I'm placing three at the base with glowing lathe-shaped domed caps and cream stems, positioning them against the stone surface.

Still writing placement code...

Checking the lathe geometry winding for the stone base — points going from [0,0] to [0.32,0] should produce correct front-facing normals matching three's vase example, so that's fine even if the bottom face is culled. I'll skip extra fluff cards for efficiency and instead consider adding small tufts near the chest/elbows area.

Now I'm scattering belly fringe tufts along the lower spine sweep where normal.y dips below -0.2, keeping them dark to match the coat tone, leaning them steeply with downward flow for a hanging fur silhouette, then layering more tufts along the back and neck for overall coverage. The card color sampling at each root point already pulls consistent belly/back coat colors. I'll skip any extra glow effects on the tail tip to keep things simple, and move on to writing a helper for the paw plate.

Writing sphere geometry helper...

Now I'm defining paint logic for the skull that marks a dark tear-line streak drifting outward below the eye and a brow spot, based on local x/y/z offsets from the head center and surface normal direction.

I'm checking that the eye region and lower-face white region don't awkwardly overlap, verifying the y-coordinate ranges against the eye's computed vertical span.

I'm checking normal.z near the sides to make sure the rust color applies correctly, picking a dark rust tone for the tear marking, and confirming the paint resolution logic uses the current surface context properly. Now I'm writing the card-scattering code for the stone/moss decals with sizing, lean, and spin parameters...

Then I move to setting up paw positions as a vector array, naming leg joints consistently (using "leg" as the role for both front and hind limbs since it's a quadruped), and working out the ribbon membrane edges as bezier paths.

Defining membrane edge curves...

Actually reconsidering the ribbon orientation—separating edges vertically rather than horizontally would make the streamer flutter more like a scarf tail seen from the side, which reads better in a 3/4 view.

For the medallion, I'll place it near the neck front using the collar loop's parameter rather than hardcoding exact coordinates. Time to preview the scene for debugging before writing the final file.
